newsitem.title: USA: Ford says yen above 110 cause for concern.
newsitem.headline: Ford says yen above 110 cause for concern.

text.p: Ford Motor Co chairman Alex Trotman said Monday that the Japanese yen as it weakens against the U.S. dollar, is an increasing cause for concern for the U.S. auto industry, particularly at the current level of about 110 yen to the dollar.
"As the yen gets weaker the threat to us (United States) gets worse by the yen," Trotman told reporters at a news conference here.

Trotman said that the yen's weakness versus the dollar has allowed Japanese automakers to be very aggressive in pricing their vehicles in the U.S. market. Many new 1997 models are priced the same as or less than the 1996 models they replace.

Trotman called the Japanese prices "quite challenging," and added that Japanese automakers have been slashing costs to allow them to be profitable in the U.S. market at an exchange rate of 85 to 90 yen to the dollar.
"That certainly does increase the competitive heat for the manufacturers here including Ford," Trotman said before a speech to the Detroit Economics Club here.
Trotman also said that U.S. car and truck sales have slowed from their brisk pace earlier this year but he added that he expects sales for the full year to end at about 15.4 million units.
In 1994, about 15.1 million vehicles were sold in the U.S.
He also said he expects 1997 U.S. vehicle sales, to be "in general terms sideways to slightly up" compared with 1996.
"I wouldn't dignify it by calling it a forecast," he said of his comments on 1997 vehicle sales.
